newsitem.title: USA: Storm emergency declared in four more U.S. counties.
newsitem.headline: Storm emergency declared in four more U.S. counties.

text.p: Washington Gov. Mike Lowry declared a state of emergency in four more counties on Monday after winter storms lashed the northwestern United States, killing four people, causing floods and blocking roads.

The declaration brought to 15 the number of Washington counties declared in emergency since Sunday because of the storms. Lowry's emergency proclamation said heavy snowfall and flooding had inflicted extensive damage on homes, businesses, roads and bridges in Cowlitz, Grays Harbor, Jefferson and Lewis counties in the west of the state.

Many rivers in Washington state, Oregon and northern California were at or above flood stage after a series of powerful storms dumped heavy snow and rain, forcing evacuations in parts of Oregon and Washington.

Washington residents dug out after the weekend's heavy storm, which disrupted travel, blocked mountain passes and left tens of thousands without electricity. Rain showers fell as residents anxiously awaited the next storm, forecast to hit by midweek.

Three deaths were blamed on the storm in Washington state, according to Mark Clemens, a spokesman for Washington State Emergency Management. Two people were killed by falling trees and a third suffocated because of a faulty heater.
An Oregon bulldozer operator drowned when his machine flipped over, Oregon state police said.

Across the border in Canada, British Columbia was also recovering from its worst blizzard in decades. A rare snowstorm dumped up to 27 inches (70 cms) during the weekend, paralyzing public transportation.

Melting snow and heavy rain caused flooding on western Washington rivers and in many urban areas, Lowry's office said. While river levels were expected to stabilize on Monday, rain storms forecast for Wednesday could bring more widespread flooding, it said.
"In many parts of the state, it is no longer the snow, but the combination of melting snow and rain that is continuing to cause damage," Lowry said.
In Seattle, office workers struggled to work through streets buried under snow and slush and most government offices allowed employees to come in two hours late.
Heavy snow brought roofs crashing down on boats at the Edmonds marina, north of Seattle, sinking 300 boats and causing an estimated $8 million damage, Clemens said.
In western Washington, some vehicles were half-submerged in flooded streets and the roofs of dozens of buildings collapsed under the weight of the snow.
Flood warnings were issued for about six rivers in western Washington state, and in Oregon a dozen rivers were at or near flood stage with water levels set to rise further.
Some 120,000 sandbags were being distributed to National Guard armories throughout Oregon.
Authorities advised residents of low-lying areas near several rivers in Thurston County around the Washington state capital of Olympia to evacuate as a precaution.
"We are advising people to evacuate now rather than later when it could be a panic situation," county spokesman Keith Eisner said. He estimated that 1,000 people had left.
The Red Cross said about 250 people spent the night at three shelters it set up in the Olympia area.

About 64,000 customers remained without power in nine counties in western Washington state, down from a peak of 248,000 on Friday, Betty Werblun, a spokeswoman for Puget Sound Power and Light Co., said.
About 7,000 customers in the Portland, Oregon, area were without electricity and about 2,000 homes and businesses in northern California were also without power.
All major mountain routes connecting western and eastern Washington state remained closed due to avalanche danger and were not expected to reopen before Wednesday.

In California, the National Weather Service issued a flood warning for the rain-swollen Napa and Russian rivers north of San Francisco and high wind warnings and flash flood watches for counties in the San Francisco Bay area.
